purpose: Acetylcysteine is used for two main reasons. It helps loosen and thin thick, sticky mucus in the lungs, making it easier to cough up, which is helpful for people with conditions like cystic fibrosis or COPD. It is also used in the emergency room as a life-saving treatment for acetaminophen (Tylenol) overdose.
how_it_works: When used for mucus, it works by breaking up the chemical bonds that make mucus thick and sticky, so it becomes thinner and easier to clear from your airways. When used for a Tylenol overdose, it works by replenishing a natural substance in your liver called glutathione, which protects liver cells from being damaged by the toxic breakdown products of too much acetaminophen. Basically, it acts as a shield to help your liver recover.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, and upset stomach are the most common side effects, especially when taken by mouth. When inhaled, it may cause a runny nose, mouth irritation, or an unpleasant rotten-egg smell. When given through an IV, some people may experience flushing, rash, or itching.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have asthma, as inhaled acetylcysteine can occasionally trigger breathing problems or wheezing. If you are receiving it by IV, watch for signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, swelling, or difficulty breathing and tell your nurse right away. Always let your healthcare team know about all other medications you take, especially if you are being treated for an overdose.
typical_dosing: For mucus: it is often inhaled using a nebulizer, typically 3 to 5 mL of a 20% solution, 3 to 4 times a day, or as directed by your doctor. For acetaminophen overdose: it is usually given by IV in a hospital setting following a specific three-bag dosing schedule over 21 hours, or it may be taken by mouth as a loading dose followed by smaller doses every few hours. Your doctor or nurse will guide you through the exact dosing.
